steps.body:
A farmer has 100 m of fence and a long straight wall. He wants the largest rectangular pen, using the wall as one side.

**Fence used** = 2x + y = 100, where x is the depth and y the width along the wall.
**Area** = xy = x(100 − 2x).

One variable, and a domain of 0 < x < 50. The wall is the whole point: it means only three sides need fencing.

explanationVariants: Three sides are fenced: two of depth x and one of width y. So 2x + y = 100 and y = 100 − 2x. The area is x(100 − 2x).
Forgetting the wall gives 2x + 2y = 100 and a completely different (and smaller) answer.

widget.prompt: 100 m of fence, three sides only (the wall is the fourth). Which area formula is right?

options.label: A = x(100 − 2x)
options.feedback: Right — two depths and one width use the fence, so y = 100 − 2x.

options.label: A = x(50 − x)
options.feedback: That is the four-sided pen, where 2x + 2y = 100 gives y = 50 − x. The wall means you only fence THREE sides, so more fence is left for the width.

options.label: A = x(100 − x)
options.feedback: That uses only ONE depth. There are two sides of length x, so the fence they consume is 2x.

options.label: A = 100x
options.feedback: That ignores the constraint entirely — it says the width is 100 no matter how deep the pen is, which would need infinite fence.

steps.body: One critical point, and the sign chart proves it is a maximum.

widget.prompt: A′(x) = 100 − 4x, a line with NEGATIVE slope. Set the signs of A′.
widget.successFeedback: + then −. The area climbs until x = 25 and falls after — so x = 25 is the maximum, and A(25) = 25 × 50 = 1250 m². Note the shape of the answer: the depth (25 + 25 = 50 m of fence) exactly equals the width (50 m). Half the fence goes each way, which is a pattern worth noticing.
widget.crossFeedback: A′ = 100 − 4x is a single root at 25, so the sign flips there — and since the leading coefficient is negative, it goes from + to −.
widget.bounceFeedback: This root is single, not repeated: A′ crosses zero rather than touching it.

cml.actionGoal: Set interval signs and use root multiplicity to explain where a function crosses or only touches the axis.

predict.prompt: A′(x) = 100 − 4x is a line with negative slope. Its sign chart will read…
predict.reveal: Positive then negative — so the area climbs, stops, and falls away: a maximum, established by the chart alone with no second derivative anywhere in sight. A line of negative slope crosses zero exactly once and only in that direction, which is why one critical point plus one sign change is already a complete argument.

explanationVariants: Both endpoints are degenerate: A(0) = 0 (no depth) and A(50) = 0 (no width).

widget.prompt: Find the maximum area of the pen, in square metres.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 50 × 50 — a square pen, which would need 150 m of fence for three sides. You only have 100.
That is 25², the depth squared. The width is 100 − 50 = 50, so the area is 25 × 50 = 1250.
That is the width y at the optimum. Multiply by the depth 25 to get the area.

steps.body:
Two habits that survive every problem of this kind:

**Check the endpoints, always.** Here they are degenerate (A = 0), but in a problem with a real constraint at the edge, the answer can live there — and a critical point that beats the interior can still lose to an edge.

**Sanity-check the shape.** Half the fence went to the two depths and half to the width. If your answer has a wildly lopsided pen, suspect an algebra slip.
When the answer IS at an endpoint.
explanationVariants: If the profit function is increasing on the whole allowed range, there is no interior critical point — the best you can do is the largest allowed value. The answer is at the endpoint.
This is exactly the EVT case from chapter 1: an endpoint maximum, with a steep tangent and no flat spot in sight.

widget.prompt: A profit function P(x) has P′(x) > 0 for every x in the allowed range [0, 40]. Where is the maximum profit?

options.label: At the right endpoint, x = 40
options.feedback: Right, and there is no critical point at all: the tangent is never flat. This is why the endpoints must ALWAYS be checked.

options.label: At no point in the interval
options.feedback: On a CLOSED interval the EVT guarantees a maximum. It just does not have to be at a critical point — here it is at the edge.

options.label: At the left endpoint, x = 0
options.feedback: That is where profit is SMALLEST: the function climbs from there all the way to 40.

options.label: At an interior point
options.feedback: An interior maximum needs f′ to change sign. Here f′ is positive throughout — the curve climbs right up to the edge.

hints: Name the variables. If the two numbers are x and 20 − x, what is the quantity to minimise?
S = x² + (20 − x)². Expand it: S = 2x² − 40x + 400.
S′ = 4x − 40 = 0 gives x = 10. Now compute S(10).
explanationVariants: Equal numbers again — and this time they MINIMISE the sum of squares, where a moment ago they maximised the product. Both facts come from the same symmetry.

widget.prompt: Two numbers add to 20. What is the SMALLEST possible sum of their squares?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 20² — what you get if one number is 0 and the other is 20. That is an ENDPOINT, and it is the maximum, not the minimum.
That is 10², the square of one number. The sum of BOTH squares is 100 + 100 = 200.
That is the value of x at the optimum. The sum of squares there is 200.

takeaways: The constraint eliminates a variable; the domain rejects the impossible answers; the derivative finds the candidates.
ALWAYS compare with the endpoints — a curve that is still climbing when the range runs out has its maximum at the edge.
Equal shares turn up again and again (10 × 10, and half the fence each way). It is worth noticing when it happens.
steps.teaser: That is curve analysis. The next course takes these derivatives out into the world: motion, related rates, and L'Hôpital's rule.

concept.body: Draw the picture and label it. Write the constraint from the picture, and the quantity you want from the picture. Then the algebra tells you what to differentiate — never the other way round.

explanationVariants: Three sides fenced: two depths (2x) and one width (y). So 2x + y = 100.
The wall is free, so it does not appear in the fence equation at all.

widget.prompt: A pen against a wall uses 100 m of fence on three sides — two of depth x, one of width y. What is the constraint?

options.label: 2x + y = 100
options.feedback: Right — the wall costs nothing, so only three sides consume fence.

options.label: 2x + 2y = 100
options.feedback: That fences all FOUR sides. The wall is already there, so the fourth side is free.
